nameStory: The Hard-fingered Sea Cucumber gets its name from the firm, finger-like projections called tentacles that surround its mouth - these 'fingers' are much more rigid than the soft, squishy tentacles of many other sea cucumber species. It's also known as the hairy sea cucumber because its body is covered in what looks like fuzzy hair, giving it a distinctly shaggy appearance underwater.
description: The Hard-fingered Sea Cucumber is a marine animal that looks like a living, breathing pickle covered in soft fuzz. Despite its name, it's not a plant at all, but an echinoderm - a relative of sea stars and sea urchins. These fascinating creatures can grow to about 4-6 inches long and have a cylindrical body with branched, tree-like tentacles around their mouth that they use to filter food from the water. Their body feels surprisingly firm to the touch, unlike the mushy texture you might expect.

idTips.label: Branched tentacles
idTips.description: Look for 8-10 tree-like tentacles around the mouth that are firm and finger-like, not soft and floppy like other sea cucumbers - they feel almost rubbery when gently touched

idTips.label: Hairy body surface
idTips.description: The entire body is covered in fine, hair-like projections that give it a fuzzy, almost velvet-like texture when you run your fingers along it

idTips.label: Cylindrical shape
idTips.description: Body is distinctly cucumber-shaped - long and rounded like a pickle, typically 4-6 inches long and about an inch thick

idTips.label: Color pattern
idTips.description: Usually brownish to reddish-brown with darker mottled patches, sometimes with a greenish tint in younger specimens

idTips.label: Firm texture
idTips.description: Body feels notably firm and somewhat rigid compared to other sea cucumbers - more like a firm sausage than a soft blob

habitat: You'll find Hard-fingered Sea Cucumbers in shallow coastal waters throughout New England, typically in rocky tide pools, under ledges, and among seaweed beds from the low tide zone down to about 30 feet deep. They prefer areas with good water flow where they can extend their tentacles to filter plankton and organic particles from the current. Look for them wedged into crevices or partially buried in sandy areas near rocks.

seasonality.spring: Most active as waters warm up, often seen with tentacles fully extended for feeding. This is when they're easiest to spot as they come out of winter hiding spots.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most likely to be found feeding actively in tide pools during low tide. Their hairy covering may appear more pronounced.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to seek more protected locations as water temperatures drop. Good time to find them under rocks and in deeper crevices.
seasonality.winter: Much less active and often hidden deep in rock crevices or buried in sediment. Rarely seen during winter tide pool exploration.

funFact: When threatened, Hard-fingered Sea Cucumbers can literally shoot their internal organs out of their body as a distraction - and then completely regrow them over the next few months, making them one of nature's most extreme escape artists!
confusionNotes: Often confused with other sea cucumbers, but remember the 'hard fingers' - their tentacles are firm and branched like tiny trees, not soft and simple like most other species. If you can gently touch the tentacles and they feel rigid rather than squishy, you've likely found a Hard-fingered Sea Cucumber.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'cucumber,' this animal is actually more closely related to sea stars and sea urchins than to any plant. The 'sea cucumber' name comes from their shape and the fact that early naturalists thought they looked like pickled cucumbers on the ocean floor.
compareHints: As the only Sclerodactyla species commonly found in New England waters, the Hard-fingered Sea Cucumber is most easily confused with other sea cucumber families. However, it stands apart from smooth sea cucumbers by its distinctly hairy body surface and from soft-tentacled species by its remarkably rigid, branched feeding tentacles. Unlike the more common smooth sea cucumbers found in New England, this species feels firm and looks fuzzy.
